title: SCAPE 2026
text: Atmospheric introduction to the Handrkov meadow: Species-rich submontane grassland ecosystem where dozens of entomophilous plants bloom simultaneously, all sharing a finite pool of flower visitors.

title: SCAPE 2026
text:
Interactions


















Start with pollination biology: In species-rich meadows, pollinators are a shared, limiting mutualistic service. Co-flowering plants do not interact in isolation; sharing insect visitors mediates indirect interactions—both facilitation (magnet plants) and competition (heterospecific pollen deposition, stigma clogging, pollen dilution). The paradox: Short-term network studies show massive year-to-year turnover and rewiring. Yet, diverse plant communities persist for decades. Is this sharing web in constant chaotic drift, or does an underlying stable architecture anchor the community?

title: SCAPE 2026
text: Step 1 (First visit links): We start from empirical flower visits in the field—an insect landing on a flower. Step 2 (Bipartite Web): As dozens of co-flowering plant species and hundreds of insect visitors interact across the meadow, these individual visits weave together into a bipartite plant-pollinator interaction network. Step 3 (Pollinator Sharing Bridge): But plants do not interact directly; they interact through the shared pool of flower visitors. When two plant species are visited by the same pollinators, those insects carry pollen between them and bridge the plants together. Step 4 (Pollinator-Sharing Network): By projecting these shared visits across the whole community, we reveal the unipartite pollinator-sharing web—a topological network of plants anchored by dense shared connections!

title: SCAPE 2026
section: Network Architecture: Airports vs. The Meadow
text:
Network Architecture: Airports vs. The Meadow



✈️ European Aviation Network

























🌸 Meadow Pollinator Sharing




















Step 0 (Title only): To understand the stability of our pollination web, let’s step outside ecology and look at an analogy from human infrastructure: the European aviation network. Step 1 (Map): Here is European airspace. Step 2 (Airports): Across Europe are 895 airports—geographically scattered, seemingly uniform. Step 3 (Routes): Add 15,000 empirical commercial flight routes—a complex topological web appears. Step 4 (Airport Coreness): Calculate coreness: a tiny core of mega-hubs (London, Amsterdam, Frankfurt, Paris) anchors continental travel, while regional airfields (Røros, Kristianstad) are peripheral spokes. Step 5 (Plant Nodes): Now look at our meadow: 57 co-flowering plant species in Handrkov. Step 6 (Plant Routes): Add empirical pollinator sharing: visitors link plants together through shared service. Step 7 (Plant Coreness): The exact same architecture emerges! Just 6 core perennial species form the central routing core, while peripheral flora connect through them.

section: What is Robustness? The Extinction Cascade
text:
What is Robustness? The Extinction Cascade






























Meadow pollinator sharing network under simulated extinction scenarios






























Co-extinction simulation (Memmott et al. 2004) on Handrkov pollination web



Slide 6: Here is how network theory formalizes robustness (Memmott et al. 2004). Step 0: Title only. Step 1 (Axes & Intact Web): Here are the co-extinction axes: proportion of plants extinct vs pollinators surviving, alongside our intact Handrkov sharing network. Step 2 (Random Loss): When species disappear at random, robustness shows a steady, intermediate decline. Step 3 (Peripheral Spoke Loss): When peripheral species are removed first (red dashed line), the curve stays flat near 100%! Almost all pollinators survive because the central core anchors them. High robustness (R ≈ 0.85). Step 4 (Core Hub Collapse): BUT when core hubs collapse (solid navy line), the curve plummets immediately! Losing Centaurea and Succisa causes massive secondary cascades. Low robustness (R ≈ 0.45). Step 5 (15-Year Question): Across 15 years, during unprecedented summer droughts, did climate stress break our core hubs, or did the core hold?

title: SCAPE 2026
text:
Macro-Dynamics: Two Decoupled Timescales




























Non-metric multidimensional scaling (NMDS) of annual directed PAC matrices (Bray-Curtis, stress = 0.106). Vector fitting identifies two decoupled, orthogonal axes: 1. Axis 1 (Horizontal - Acute Climate Pulse): Summer drought severity (r² = 0.55, p = 0.008) and summer temperature (r² = 0.67, p = 0.001) displace the network during severe droughts (2015 and 2018) far to the right into centralized topological states. 2. Axis 2 (Vertical - Decadal Press): Steady successional progression across 15 years (r² = 0.71, p = 0.0008). Crucially: Notice the hysteresis! When rainfall returned in 2020-2021, the network shifted back horizontally along Axis 1, but NEVER returned to its pre-2015 baseline along Axis 2.

title: SCAPE 2026
text:
Identifying the Meadow’s Permanent Hubs


Are the network hubs just an ephemeral accident of whoever happens to produce the most flowers in a given year?

Or does the meadow possess a permanent set of topological anchors that maintain core roles across 15 years—irrespective of climatic extremes?


Recall our airport analogy: is Frankfurt an international hub because it randomly had an extra runway open on a sunny Tuesday? Or because of permanent structural routing? In pollination networks, the central question is whether network hubs are merely abundant generalists, or whether specific plant identities provide permanent community cohesion. To test this, we compared every species against a presence-conditional null model across all 15 years.

title: SCAPE 2026
text:
Discovering the True Core






Are network hubs just random flowers that happen to bloom heavily? We tested each species’ 15-year standardized coreness against a conservative, presence-conditional (flowering-only) null model (1,000 perms/yr). Exactly 6 species maintained statistically significant excess centrality: Centaurea jacea, Selinum carvifolia, Succisa pratensis, Pimpinella saxifraga, Achillea ptarmica, and Ranunculus acris (all P_adj <= 0.0015).

title: SCAPE 2026
section: Plant Identity Matters: Not an Abundance Lottery!
text:
Plant Identity Matters: Not an Abundance Lottery!


The Neutral Hypothesis

Hubs are just whichever plants produce the most flowers.
Coreness drifts randomly with plant density.
Species traits play no role.


Linear Mixed Model (Centrality)

Plant Identity: explains 38% of variance
Floral Abundance: explains 44% of variance
LRT for Plant Identity:
\(\chi^2 = 328.8, \mathbf{p = 1.8 \times 10^{-73}}\)





Pollinators actively seek out core species beyond their sheer floral abundance.
The core is an enduring architectural feature grounded in intrinsic floral syndromes and attractiveness.



Even after controlling for raw flower count, species identity explains nearly 40% of the variance. Topological invariance: In multi-year modularity cartography (Guimerà & Amaral), these exact same 6 species emerge as permanent module hubs (z = 0.86-2.39). Markov role transitions show core species have a 59.2% probability of remaining hubs year-to-year and a 70.4% rebound probability, compared to only 3.5% for peripherals.

title: SCAPE 2026
text:
Secondary Extinctions: The Fragility Flip























We simulated secondary extinction cascades (Memmott et al. 2004). Robustness R is the area under the co-extinction curve. During normal years: The meadow exhibits high structural redundancy (R ≈ 0.63–0.84). During severe droughts (2015, 2018): Core loss triggers catastrophic collapse (R ≈ 0.45), while peripheral loss is easily buffered (R ≈ 0.83). The Robustness Gap (ΔR) surges! In drought years, network survival becomes almost exclusively dependent on the 6 core species.

title: SCAPE 2026
text:
Rising Vulnerability: Core Dependence (\(\Delta R\))






Core dependence (\(\Delta R = R_{\text{periph}} - R_{\text{core}}\)) surges during acute summer droughts (\(p = 0.018\)) and steadily intensifies over time (\(+0.022/\text{yr}, p = 0.014\)).


Slide: Core dependence surges during droughts and steadily rises across 15 years. When severe droughts strike, losing the core causes far more catastrophic secondary cascades than losing peripheral species.

title: SCAPE 2026
text:
The Ecological Driver: Floral Asymmetry






The Life-Raft Mechanism: Peripheral displays crash 10-fold (\(\beta = -28.0, p = 0.032\)), while the core remains completely drought-buffered (\(\beta = +0.9, p = 0.792\)) \(\rightarrow\) pollinators concentrate on core heads, making them the community’s sole life-support system.


Slide: Why does the network become so dependent on the core? Profound floral asymmetry: peripheral flowers collapse 10-fold during extreme droughts, whereas the 6 core perennial species maintain steady floral displays. Pollinators are forced onto the core life-raft!

title: SCAPE 2026
text:
Take-Home Messages for Pollination Ecology




01 • Architecture


Dynamic Web,Persistent Anchor


High annual rewiring is anchored by a permanent core of 6 plant species.  Centrality is driven by plant identity (explaining 38% of variance), not an abundance lottery.






02 • Mechanism


The Life-RaftBuffer


Severe drought triggers a 10-fold crash in peripheral flowers, while core plants remain buffered.  Pollinators crowd onto the core, turning it into the community’s sole life-support system.







03 • Implication


TargetedConservation


Preserving network resilience against climate extremes requires safeguarding keystone plants that unite:


High floral attractiveness


Deep drought tolerance








Architecture: The 15-year dataset reveals that network coreness is topologically invariant and identity-based (LMM p = 1.8e-73, explaining 38% of centrality variance after controlling for flower abundance).
Mechanism: Extinction cascade simulations demonstrate a catastrophic robustness drop (R = 0.45) if core is lost during drought. Peripheral flowers collapse 10-fold (p = 0.032), but core plants flower unaffected (p = 0.792).
Conservation: Grassland management must focus beyond simple species counts to protect these dual-trait keystone species (e.g. Centaurea, Succisa, Selinum) that guarantee network survival during extreme climatic shocks.
